title: Meet the OS
about: What the operating system manages, ending frozen apps, and safe updates.

cards.prompt: Music, a game and a message ping all want the **speaker** at once.

choices.text: The first app to grab it keeps it
choices.consequence: Then the music would hog the speaker, and you'd never hear the ping.

choices.text: Each app uses it whenever it likes
choices.consequence: Three apps driving one speaker at once would clash. Something has to share it out.

choices.text: One main program shares it out fairly
choices.consequence: Yes. The ping plays over the music, and the game's sounds too.

cards.explanation: Apps share the [[CPU]], [[RAM]], screen and speaker, so one main program shares them out: the **operating system**.
cards.hint: Think of a referee: should players grab the ball, or should someone share out turns?

cards.title: The operating system
cards.body:
That main program is the **operating system** (**OS**), the referee:

- It gives apps quick turns on the [[CPU]], so they seem to run at once.
- It shares out [[RAM]] and keeps apps out of each other's data.
- It talks to the **hardware** (screen, keyboard, Wi-Fi) for them.

cards.prompt: Whose job is it: the **operating system's**, or an **app's**?

items.label: Decide which app uses the CPU next
Share out RAM between open apps
Talk to the keyboard, screen and Wi-Fi
Stop apps reading each other's data
Add a funny filter to a selfie

cards.explanation: The **OS** manages what every app shares: CPU time, RAM, hardware and safety. **Apps** each do one job for you.
cards.hint: Is it about sharing something every app needs, or one job an app does for you?
cards.nudge: The OS handles shared things like CPU turns, RAM and [[hardware]]; apps do one job for you.

cards.prompt: This **task manager** lists each **process** (a running program). End the one hogging the [[CPU]]; keep music and [[browser]] open, and never end **System** (the OS).
cards.explanation: The **drawing app** was hogging 85% of the CPU, so ending it fixed the freeze. Ending **System** would have crashed the laptop.
cards.hint: Compare the CPU numbers: which process takes far more than the rest?
cards.nudge: End only the CPU hog; keep the music, the browser and **System** running.

cards.prompt: One app keeps grabbing [[RAM]] (a **memory leak**). Slide time to **40 min or more**, then end it. Keep the music on.
cards.explanation: The **chat app** grew by 0.15 GB a minute, to 6.5 GB after 40 minutes. Ending or restarting it gives the RAM back.
cards.hint: Slide time forward, then find the app whose RAM keeps growing.
cards.nudge: A leaky app's RAM keeps climbing; don't end the music or **System**.

cards.prompt: **Updates** fix mistakes (**bugs**) and weak spots attackers use (**security holes**). You're mid-essay.

steps.text: A pop-up says **"Updates are ready. Restart now?"**

choices.consequence: The unsaved essay was only in [[RAM]], so restarting wiped it.

choices.text: Save the essay first, then restart
choices.consequence: The essay is safe in [[storage]], and the update can start.
Then the security holes stay open, and your laptop gets less safe.

steps.text: The screen says **"Working on updates. Don't turn off your device."** It's been ten minutes.

choices.text: Hold the power button to stop it
choices.consequence: Cutting an update off halfway can leave the OS unable to start.

choices.text: Plug in the charger and let it finish
choices.consequence: Big updates take a while. Staying powered lets it finish safely.

cards.explanation: **Save your work**, then let updates finish with the charger in. Switching off halfway can break the OS.
cards.hint: Where does unsaved work live, and what happens to it on a restart?

cards.prompt: Your screen flashes red. Good to know: a web page can't see what's on your laptop.

steps.text: **"WARNING! Your laptop has 5 [[viruses|virus]]! Download CleanerPro now or call this number!"**

choices.consequence: Pop-ups like this are fakes. The "cleaner" is usually the harmful program itself.

choices.text: Call the number on the screen
choices.consequence: It's a scam. The caller will ask for money or for control of your laptop.

choices.text: Don't click anything; close the tab
choices.consequence: A web page knowing what's on your laptop is like a billboard knowing what's in your fridge. It's fake.

steps.text: The page keeps popping back up and the tab won't close.

choices.text: End the browser in task manager; tell an adult
choices.consequence: The page is gone, and they can help you check everything is fine.

choices.text: Click the pop-up's "Cancel" to close it
choices.consequence: Buttons on a fake pop-up can do anything, including start a download.

cards.explanation: A web page can't see your files, so the warning is **fake**. Close the browser (with the task manager if needed) and tell a parent, teacher or someone you trust.
cards.hint: Can a web page really see what's on your laptop?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- The **OS** is the referee: it shares out CPU, RAM and hardware.
- Frozen app? End its process in the task manager, never System.
- Save your work, then let updates finish.

Next: where your files actually live.
